pages.body:
Look closely at your hand, then look at a photo of a cat or a fish. All living things look different on the outside. But they are all built from the same kind of tiny building block.

- Every living thing you can name is made up of parts too small to see with your eyes alone.
- Scientists call these building blocks cells.

All animals, including humans, are made up of cells. A cell is the smallest working unit of a living thing. Cells are very small. You need a microscope or a strong magnifier to see most of them.

An animal cell has several parts. Each part is called an organelle, and each organelle does its own job, just like organs do a job inside your body.

pages.body:
| **Part of the cell** | **What it does** |
|---|---|
| Cell membrane | A thin skin around the cell. It controls what enters and leaves the cell. |
| Cytoplasm | A soft fluid that fills the cell. Many of the cell's activities happen here. |
| Nucleus | The control centre of the cell. It holds the instructions that direct everything the cell does. |
| Ribosome | A tiny structure that makes proteins for the cell. |
| Endoplasmic reticulum | A network of tubes that moves proteins and other substances around inside the cell. |
| Golgi apparatus | Packages proteins and other materials, then ships them to where they are needed. |
| Mitochondrion | Releases the energy the cell needs to work. A cell may have many of these. |
| Lysosome | Breaks down waste and worn out parts inside the cell. |
| Vacuole | A small storage space. It stores water and waste for a short time. |
> **Every animal cell has a nucleus, a cell membrane and cytoplasm.**

parts.a: For example: cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, ribosome, mitochondrion (also endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosome, vacuole).

pages.body:
A mango tree can grow taller than a house, yet it cannot walk to find water like an animal can. It must stand firm in the wind and rain, and it must make its own food from sunlight.

Look at the picture below. It shows what the thin skin of an onion looks like under a microscope. Notice how neat and box-like the cells are.

[[img:isbojusz2]]
[[img:i1bobo8e3]]

Think about it. What might a plant's cells need that an animal's cells do not?

- Something to keep the plant standing firm and strong, and its cells boxy in shape.
- Something to help the plant catch sunlight and turn it into food.

Plants are also made up of cells. A plant cell has the same basic parts as an animal cell, but it also has three extra parts that help the plant stay firm and make its own food.

[[img:ipd9ltuj5]]

pages.body:
| **Part of the cell** | **What it does** |
|---|---|
| Cell wall | A strong, stiff layer outside the cell membrane. It gives the cell a fixed shape and keeps the plant firm. |
| Cell membrane | A thin skin inside the cell wall. It controls what enters and leaves the cell. |
| Cytoplasm | A soft fluid that fills the cell, where many activities take place. |
| Nucleus | The control centre of the cell. |
| Ribosome | A tiny structure that makes proteins for the cell. |
| Endoplasmic reticulum | A network of tubes that moves proteins and other substances around inside the cell. |
| Golgi apparatus | Packages proteins and other materials, then ships them to where they are needed. |
| Mitochondrion | Releases the energy the cell needs to work. |
| Large vacuole | A big storage space filled with cell sap. It keeps the cell firm and full of water. |
| Chloroplast | Traps sunlight and uses it to make food for the plant. Animal cells do not have this part. |
> **A cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts are found only in plant cells.**

pages.body:
You have now studied an animal cell and a plant cell. Before you read on, try this on your own.

- Fold a page in your notebook into two columns. Head one column Animal Cell and the other Plant Cell.
- From memory, write down as many parts as you can remember under each column.
- Circle any part that appears in both columns.

Animal cells and plant cells are alike in many ways because both are built from the same basic type of unit, the cell. But they are not exactly the same. A plant needs to stay firm in one place and make its own food, so its cells have a few extra parts that an animal cell does not need.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What they share, how they differ

pages.title: What animal cells and plant cells share
pages.body:
- Both have a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
- Both have cytoplasm, the soft fluid that fills the cell.
- Both have a nucleus that controls the cell's activities.
- Both have mitochondria that release energy for the cell.
- Both have ribosomes, an endoplasmic reticulum and a Golgi apparatus, which work together to make and package proteins.
- Both have at least one vacuole for storage.

pages.title: How they are different
pages.body:
| **Feature** | **Animal cell** | **Plant cell** |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Absent | Present. Gives the cell a fixed, boxy shape |
| Chloroplast | Absent | Present. Traps sunlight to make food |
| Vacuole | Small, and there may be several | One very large vacuole that fills most of the cell |
| Overall shape | Round or irregular, since there is no cell wall | Fixed and often box-like, because of the cell wall |

> **A cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole are the three parts that make a plant cell different from an animal cell.**

pages.body:
- All living things are made up of cells, the smallest working units of life.
- An animal cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, ribosomes, an endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes and small vacuoles.
- A plant cell has all the same basic parts as an animal cell, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and one large vacuole.
- The cell wall gives a plant cell its fixed, box-like shape and keeps the plant firm.
- Chloroplasts trap sunlight so the plant can make its own food.
- Animal and plant cells share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, an endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus and at least one vacuole.

| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Cell | The smallest working unit of a living thing |
| Organelle | A small part inside a cell that does a particular job |
| Cell membrane | The thin skin around a cell that controls what enters and leaves |
| Cytoplasm | The soft fluid that fills a cell |
| Nucleus | The control centre of the cell |
| Nucleolus | A small round part inside the nucleus |
| Ribosome | A tiny structure that makes proteins |
| Endoplasmic reticulum | A network of tubes that moves substances around inside the cell |
| Golgi apparatus | The organelle that packages and ships materials made in the cell |
| Mitochondrion | The organelle that releases energy for the cell to use |
| Lysosome | The organelle that breaks down waste inside the cell |
| Vacuole | A storage space inside a cell that holds water, food or waste |
| Cell wall | The strong, stiff layer outside a plant cell's membrane |
| Chloroplast | The organelle in a plant cell that traps sunlight to make food |

pages.title: From cells to organisms
pages.body:
A cell is the smallest working unit of a living thing, but cells rarely work alone. Cells of the same kind that work together to do one job form a tissue. Muscle tissue, for example, is made of muscle cells. Different tissues join to form an organ such as the heart or a leaf. Organs that work together form an organ system such as the digestive system, and all the systems together make up the organism.

- Cell, the basic unit, for example a muscle cell.
- Tissue, a group of similar cells doing one job, for example muscle tissue.
- Organ, different tissues working together, for example the heart.
- Organ system, organs working together, for example the circulatory system.
- Organism, the whole living thing.

Some organisms are made of only one cell and are called unicellular organisms. Amoeba and bacteria are examples. Organisms made of many cells, such as humans, goats and mango trees, are called multicellular organisms. New cells are made when existing cells divide, which is how a multicellular organism grows and repairs damaged parts.

parts.a: A unicellular organism is made of only one cell, for example amoeba or bacteria. A multicellular organism is made of many cells, for example humans, goats or mango trees.
